report:
**Conclusion: the claim is well supported.** The key evidence is the phase 3 ACTIVE randomized, double-blind trial in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. At 18 months, new vertebral fractures occurred in **0.6%** of women assigned daily subcutaneous abaloparatide versus **4.2%** with placebo (*p*<0.0001): an absolute reduction of about **3.6 percentage points** and relative reduction of about **86%**. This directly supports the stated claim. The FDA-approved label reports the same endpoint and also notes consistent vertebral/nonvertebral fracture reductions across baseline age, time since menopause, prior-fracture status, and bone-density subgroups.  
https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=712143d9-e21e-4013-bb3b-3426a21060a8&audience=consumer  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/208743s003lbl.pdf  

The underlying trial’s conclusion was that abaloparatide, compared with placebo, reduced new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures over 18 months in this population.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640  

Independent synthesis is directionally consistent: a network meta-analysis concluded that abaloparatide reduces vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk versus placebo and other options in postmenopausal osteoporosis.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6614166/  

**Important context:** the evidence is strongest for women resembling trial participants—postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and appreciable fracture risk—and for an 18‑month treatment period. It demonstrates fewer *new morphometric vertebral fractures* (radiographically detected), not that every individual will benefit equally. Clinical prescribing also requires weighing adverse effects, contraindications, duration limits, and follow-on osteoporosis therapy with a clinician.
